newsitem.title: INDIA: India fire toll 204; investigators start grim task.
newsitem.headline: India fire toll 204; investigators start grim task.

text.p: The death toll from a gruesome religious campsite fire in this eastern Indian town rose to 204 on Tuesday, and investigators began the grim task of sifting through the ashes for clues to the disaster.

Santosh Upadhyaya, the Superintendent of Police in this dusty town in the coastal state of Orissa, said the death toll was likely to rise because most of the survivors had sustained burns to 30 to 90 percent of their bodies.
Doctors at Baripada's hospital said four more victims had died overnight of burns, taking the death toll to 204. Doctors were battling to save more than 180 seriously-injured survivors.

Upadhyaya told Reuters state authorities were planning to enlist forensic experts for the probe into the inferno that ripped through makeshift bamboo and straw shelters where 15,000 devotees of a Hindu saint had gathered for a three-day festival.

The police chief said early investigations showed the devastating blaze was caused by a short-circuit in the hastily-erected electrical system rigged up in a football ground that was once a cremation ground for a local ruler.

"It was basically caused by an electrical short-circuit. There is no question of a gas cylinder explosion," Upadhyaya said, referring to early reports that the blaze might have been caused by an exploding cooking-gas canister.
Upadhyaya said smoking was strictly prohibited at the campsite.
Nirmal Kishore Biswal, one of the organisers of the meeting, said it was a tradition of the Thakur Nigamananda sect to build bamboo and straw shelters for the annual congregations.
Biswal said 50 truckloads of straw were used to build the rough shelters and provide bedding for the male devotees who died on Sunday afternoon during a post-lunch siesta.

On Monday evening authorities began the grim task of mass cremations for unidentified victims of the fire, the deadliest fire in India since December 1995 when about 425 people died in flames and smoke that engulfed a school prizegiving ceremony in the northern town of Dabwali.
Officials said the fire underlined a disregard for fire safety in India, which has no federal fire regulations.

"Indeed, it is inexplicable that despite the huge popular enthusiasm that pilgrimages and religious meets generate in this country, hardly any attention is paid to crowd management," New Delhi's Pioneer newspaper wrote in an angry Monday editorial.

"As a result disasters like the one witnessed at Baripada keep occurring with the respective state governments at the very most doling out a few thousand rupees to the families of those deceased," the newspaper said.
Thousands of grieving relatives watched on Monday night as rescue workers shifted corpses charred beyond recognition from the site of Sunday's inferno to pyres at a nearby cremation ground.
Priests chanted Hindu hymns as bodies piled five to a pyre burned on the banks of the River Burhabalanga.
Sunday's blaze, fanned by gusting winds, spared a separate section for women and children.
"There was hardly any time to escape as the fire burnt down the camp within three minutes," said 27-year-old Dilip Kumar Mohapatra, who was recovering in a Cuttack hospital.
"There was a near-stampede because everyone was trying to get out of the only gate."

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda flew to the spot on Monday to announce federal payments of 50,000 rupees ($1,400) to the victims' families and 25,000 rupees ($700) to the injured. The aid came on top of state payments of 25,000 rupees to the families of the deceased and 10,000 rupees to the injured.
